FCHl2ybdAm.figureCaption: Figure 1: RoLA transforms a single in-the-wild image into an interactive, physics-enabled robotic environment. Given a single input image (top-left), RoLA recovers the physical scene for robot learning (top-right), enables large-scale robotic data generation (bottom-right), and supports de- ployment of learned policies on real robots (bottom-left).

FdgtV9mO6j.figureCaption: Figure 1: The overall pipeline of our method. We mark components related to humans in yellow, components related to physical information and decision making of the robot in blue, and fused features in green. We use ACI to quantify the prediction uncertainty of human trajectories and con- catenate these metrics with predictions before inputting them into networks. The networks contain attention mechanisms for interactions between humans (H-H attention) and between humans and the ego robot (H-R attention). Prediction uncertainty combined with physical information is used for designing costs. EXgckdYESp.figureCaption: Figure 1: An overview of our proposed PicoPose with a three-stage pixel-to-pixel correspondence learning process for novel object pose estimation from RGB images. With zero-shot capability, PicoPose enables rapid deployment across various robotic manipulation systems for unseen objects.

EBcb4LemZZ.figureCaption: Figure 1: We introduce a co-design framework that jointly optimizes the spatial stiffness distribution and grasp- ing poses of soft grippers via a simulation-trained neural surrogate. Hardware experiments demonstrate that our optimized grippers outperform both rigid and overly compliant designs.

E9t1ekt6W9.figureCaption: Figure 1: Framework Overview. We consider robotic systems composed of a model-free diffusion planner and a model-based optimization module. In this example, the diffusion policy is trained on right-skewed goal-reaching behaviors, while the model-based module can only correct plans to the right. The key challenge is to jointly sample a plan and its correction such that both modules are aware of each other’s capabilities. We propose Joint Model-based Model-free Diffusion (JM2D), which defines an interaction potential combining the diffusion model, optimization module, and constraints. Starting from joint noise, our method denoises both components together, yielding mutually compatible samples (green box). In contrast, conventional sequential sampling fails to account for the optimization module’s limitations, resulting in misaligned outputs (purple box).

DzRNBBCP4R.figureCaption: Figure 1: RAD learns from human and robot data through reasoning. EgSDP6AOF1.figureCaption: Figure 1: Universal Skill representations (UniSkill) are cross-embodiment skill representations shared across various embodiments (e.g., humans, Franka, WidowX) trained from both human and robot videos via skill dynamics modeling. UniSkill, trained on large-scale cross-embodiment videos, learns an embodiment-agnostic skill representation that enables interpreting human videos as skill sequences executable directly through a skill-conditioned policy.

9f3klkpa4y.figureCaption: Figure 1: Comparison between Behavior Cloning (BC) and Contrastive Learning via Action Sequence Supervision (CLASS). 7XyO9Y1hI1.figureCaption: Figure 1: EndoVLA enables robust autonomous tracking in endoscopic procedures, demonstrating effective zero-shot generalization capabilities across general scenes and sequential tracking tasks. ular reflections that cause rapidly changing appearances. These factors render conventional vision- based tracking pipelines brittle, as they typically decompose the task into distinct perception, motion planning, and control modules—each requiring manual tuning and lacking the ability to generalize across diverse anatomical scenes and incorporate high-level surgical intent [10, 11]. To tackle these constraints, learning-based strategies such as reinforcement learning have been proposed to address specific endoscopic tasks, aiming to improve precision and outcomes [12, 13, 14, 15]. However, these approaches often require intensive data, detailed reward engineering, and extensive parameter tuning. Tk20sRMzhv.figureCaption: Figure 1: End-effector robot-mediated rehabilitation platform. Users’ forces along each positional axis are mapped to the corresponding x/y/z velocity of an on-screen avatar ball (c), where the z axis into and out of the screen is represented by a decrease and increase in avatar size, respectively. Users are instructed to follow a target ball along a displayed trajectory. Force and game trajectory data (of both avatar and target) are collected at 1000 Hz and 60 Hz, respectively. During this process, two Trigno Quattro 4-channel sensor motes (d), controlled through a Trigno Base Station (Delsys, Inc., Natick, MA, USA) collect surface electromyography (sEMG) data at a rate of 2.22 kHz from 8 upper limb muscles (e). Electrode placements are as follows: anterior deltoid (AD), middle deltoid (MD), posterior deltoid (PD), and biceps brachii (BB), grounded at the acromion (G1); and triceps brachii (long head, TR), brachioradialis (BR), wrist flexors (FL), and wrist extensors (EX), grounded at the olecranon (G2). All data are collected and synchronized via Redis (MongoDB, Inc., New York, NY, USA). Full implementation details are included with code release.

PAX622BSf6.figureCaption: Figure 1: REAP learns which symbolically applicable actions are geometrically feasible, without modeling the geometric constraints. (1) Grasping the target o1 is symbolically applicable, but not geometrically feasible since other objects block the target. (2) A relational GNN, whose input state includes the goal, predicts a cost Q(s, a) for each applicable action and applies to any number of objects. Feasible picks of blocking objects get low costs, infeasible picks high costs. (3) At test time, a plan is found by greedy execution or greedy best-first search on Q, with the motion planner checking each expanded action. Q is learned by an RL algorithm that uses ε-greedy WA⋆to guide the exploration and penalizes infeasible actions.

rfRjWMFfvV.figureCaption: Figure 1: Local skills are not enough for dual-robot coordination. hWuk4y2AeR.figureCaption: Figure 1: DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO addresses long-horizon multi- object rearrangement by using progressive-widening Monte Carlo Tree Search over continuous actions. Using an initial behavior-cloned policy to propose short-horizon actions, DISCO expands search trees in parallel GPU simulation to discover long-horizon plans. The search trees are then distilled into a policy and a value function, enabling direct rollout on held-out tasks, such as real-world shelf packing. MCTS and simulation are used only during training. At test time, the distilled model acts directly from point clouds.

OJkazbkLtE.figureCaption: Figure 1: FLEX overview. A human’s task instruction (left) results in a misalignment between the human’s (green) and robot’s (lavender) internal task representations. To address this misalignment, FLEX receives natural language corrections and applies three operations (orange) to ADD missing features, GENERALIZE overly specific features, and MASK irrelevant features. zr63f3tmyq.figureCaption: Figure 1: Overview of MAST-VLA. MAST-VLA introduces two complementary conditioning paths for multi-skill VLA policies: skill-conditioned LoRA-MoE adaptation in the LLM backbone and a trajectory-affordance spatial prior in the action head. The expanded LLM-block view shows FFN-side LoRA-MoE routing with skill-conditioned routing bias, while the action-head view shows how the predicted affordance heatmap is converted into a patch-level spatial prior for action gener- ation. capacity with primitive manipulation skills, making it difficult to separate skill-specific action pat- terns and control preferences within a shared policy [24, 25, 22, 26]. For interaction-level ground- ing, low-dimensional action supervision provides only indirect cues about contact regions, motion trends, and task-relevant geometry, whereas prior manipulation methods have shown the importance of explicit spatial, geometric, or affordance-level signals [27, 16, 17, 18, 28, 29]. Thus, multi-skill VLA policies require mechanisms that preserve shared visual-language knowledge while explicitly conditioning adaptation on primitive skills and strengthening action-relevant spatial supervision.

EAeJdjpDzM.figureCaption: Figure 1: Optimization-guided diffusion. A task-space diffusion prior generates an initial reverse denoising step. Instead of sampling the standard DDIM perturbation ωk, we replace it with a structured correction δk obtained from a constrained optimization problem. The objective minimizes the perturbation magnitude while incorporating embodiment- and environment-specific costs and constraints, such as J, Xtarget, and Xinit. By changing only this constraint module, the same frozen prior can be reused across different manipulators.

VLS demonstrates excellent performance in simulation benchmarks as well as real-world experiments, proving its effectiveness.

The current observation stream is encoded by the VLM, while AdaRMS combines ˆct with the flow-time embedding to generate per-layer modulation parameters for the DiT action expert, so the predicted action vector field is explicitly conditioned on the estimated training condition.

dE7KjOl8yu.figureCaption: Figure 1: Multi-modal, high-fidelity and controllable sensor emulation. Robotic simulation pipelines often focus on scene content, overlooking physically accurate sensor modeling. VisionSIM aims to bridge this gap by emulating diverse sensor types and their failure modes. (Top) A single scene is rendered once with dense ground truth — color, depth, optical flow, surface normals, segmentation, point map, direct and indirect illumination, and a temperature map. (Middle) The same scene is then replayed through a breadth of sensor models. (Bottom) Each model exposes and enables sweeping across the sensor’s physical parameters (e.g., thermal time constant, correlation function, event thresholds), thereby reproducing modality-specific failure modes.
